title: In Mexico, some radishes are grown to be carved, not eaten
hook: The contest radishes Oaxaca grows aren't fit to eat

open.title: Why radish carvings fill a Mexican square for one night
open.line: Every December 23, radish carvings go up in a square in Oaxaca.

summary: Since 1897, Oaxaca, Mexico has held a radish carving contest every December 23. The radishes are inedible, and carvings wilt fast, so they're shown only a few hours.

text: On December 23, radish carvings line the main square in Oaxaca, Mexico.
Most are scenes made of several radishes.
In 1897, the mayor made it radish carving contest day.
It's yearly, and it's called the Night of the Radishes.

panels.text: Why carve a radish? Just eat it.

text: The city grows them on its own plot.
They stay in the ground long past harvest.
Actually, they aren't grown to be eaten.
Heavy fertilizer and chemicals make them unfit to eat.
They grow up to 50 cm long and 3 kg.
Rows are planted every few weeks for varied sizes. That also stops cheating.
Radishes are handed out on the 18th,
and all carving and setup happens on the 23rd.
So they last only a few evening hours. Lines can take 4 to 5 hours.
In 2014, 12 tons of radishes were pulled for one night.
Judging ends around 9 pm, and the carvings are soon cleared.

sources: Smithsonian Magazine: Why Radish Carving Has Become a Popular Holiday Event in Oaxaca (2018)
